```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment='#>',fig.width=8,fig.height=4.8,dpi=120)
options(rgl.useNULL=TRUE)
library(linf)
stopifnot(requireNamespace('ivue',quietly=TRUE))
label.set<-function(ids,fit) vapply(strsplit(ids,',',fixed=TRUE),function(j)
  paste(fit$feature.labels[as.integer(j)],collapse=' + '),character(1))
```

## Start with the meaning of a state

A **pure unordered top-2 state** groups observations with the same two leading
features, regardless of which is first. Here “pure” means the original rank-based
assignment, not that only two taxa are present. A pure top-3 state uses three
leading features. Neither is a VALENCIA classifier label.

The same memberships support two different graphs:

| Graph | Vertex | Edge |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Taxon graph, as used for the VME feature display | A taxon | A selected pair state containing its two endpoint taxa |
| Pair-state graph from `linf.udcst.graph()` | A pure pair state | Two overlapping pair states, optionally requiring observed support from their common leading triple |

An edge's sample count in the first graph is not the same quantity as its
support in the second. We will build both from inspectable synthetic rows,
then repeat the counting on bundled vaginal microbiome data. These graphs
summarize membership; they do not establish ecological interaction or temporal
transitions.

## Twelve observations you can inspect

The four columns A–D stand for taxa. Entries are arbitrary nonnegative
abundances; their scale within a row does not change the ranking. All rows
have at least three positive entries.

```{r toy-data}
X<-rbind(c(6,3,1,0),c(3,6,1,0),c(7,2,1,0),c(2,7,1,0),c(6,3,0,1),
         c(6,1,3,0),c(3,1,6,0),c(6,0,3,1),c(0,6,3,1),c(0,3,6,1),
         c(6,1,0,3),c(1,0,6,3))
colnames(X)<-LETTERS[1:4];rownames(X)<-paste0('s',seq_len(nrow(X)))
pair<-linf.udcsts(X,level=2,n0=1,low.freq.policy='pure')
triple<-linf.udcsts(X,level=3,n0=1,low.freq.policy='pure')
knitr::kable(data.frame(Sample=rownames(X),X,
  Pair=label.set(pair$pure.id,pair),Triple=label.set(triple$pure.id,triple)),row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(pair$pure.id,linf.udcsts(normalize.linf(X),2,1,'pure')$pure.id))
```

For example, s1 and s2 have opposite dominance orders but belong to the same
A + B pair state. Multiplying a row by a positive constant, including L1 or
max normalization, leaves these rank-based memberships unchanged.

Exact abundance ties use original column order. IDs such as `1,2` refer to
column indices and must travel with their feature dictionary. A row with
fewer than two or three positive features still receives a complete set,
with zero-valued ranks resolved by that tie rule. Check `positive.features`
before interpreting such a label as evidence that every named taxon is present.

## Coverage selects whole states, not abundance within a sample

Suppose we request 60% coverage. We order pure pair states by their number of
observations, then retain complete frequency tiers until reaching at least
60% of all input rows. Equal-frequency states are retained together, so the
achieved coverage can overshoot the request.

```{r coverage}
g60<-linf.udcst.graph(X,coverage=60)
ft<-pair$frequency.table
knitr::kable(data.frame(State=label.set(ft$ID,pair),n=ft$freq,
  Percent=100*ft$freq/nrow(X),Cumulative_tier_percent=ft$cumm.pct,
  Selected=ft$ID %in% g60$nodes$ID),digits=2,row.names=FALSE)
```

A + B contains five observations and A + C contains three. Together they
cover **8/12 = 66.67%**. This says nothing about whether A and B together
account for 60% of s1's abundance. It also does not change any coordinates.

```{r coverage-tiers, fig.cap="Coverage changes in whole frequency tiers. The 90% request retains both singleton states and reaches 100%."}
requested<-c(40,60,80,90,100)
coverage.table<-do.call(rbind,lapply(requested,function(q) {
  g<-linf.udcst.graph(X,coverage=q)
  data.frame(Request=q,Achieved=g$metadata$coverage,States=nrow(g$nodes))
}))
plot(coverage.table$Request,coverage.table$Achieved,type='b',pch=16,lwd=2,
  xlim=c(35,100),ylim=c(35,100),col='#0072B2',xlab='Requested coverage (%)',
  ylab='Achieved coverage (%)')
abline(0,1,lty=2,col='gray55')
knitr::kable(coverage.table,digits=2,row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(g60$metadata$selected.n==8L,all(coverage.table$Achieved>=requested))
```

## Filtering and absorption are additional decisions

Coverage by itself selects states. It does not assign every remaining sample
to them. `linf.udcsts()` offers three explicit rare-state policies at a
minimum frequency `n0`: preserve pure membership and mark rare rows, filter
those rows through a mask, or absorb them into retained sets.

The following uses the frequency cutoff selected by the 60% request.
Under **linf's unordered absorption rule**, a rare row is assigned to the
retained pair with the largest sum of its feature abundances. Ties use the
lexicographic order of numerical column-index tuples. This is not a
nearest-neighbor rule and is not a reproduction of VME's multi-stage
reference-based assignment procedure.

```{r absorption}
absorbed<-linf.udcsts(X,2,g60$metadata$n0,'absorb')
filtered<-linf.udcsts(X,2,g60$metadata$n0,'filter')
assignment.table<-data.frame(Sample=rownames(X),Pure=label.set(pair$pure.id,pair),
  Assigned=label.set(absorbed$assignment,absorbed),Status=absorbed$status)
knitr::kable(assignment.table,row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(sum(filtered$keep)==8L,all(absorbed$keep),
  identical(absorbed$pure.id,pair$pure.id),sum(absorbed$status=='absorbed')==4L)
```

All twelve rows now have an active assignment, but **pure core coverage is
still 66.67%**. For s9, the original leading pair is B + C and A is absent;
its active assignment is nevertheless A + B because that retained pair wins
the specified score. Keeping both columns prevents the merged label from
being mistaken for the original leading pair. Neither operation modifies X.

## A taxon graph and its vertex statistics

For the VME-style representation, use taxa as vertices and selected pure
pair states as edges. We draw the retained family on a circle to make the
connectivity visible. This is a schematic, not an abundance embedding.

```{r taxon-summary}
taxon.stats<-function(fit,ids,assignment=fit$pure.id) {
  sets<-fit$feature.sets[match(ids,fit$pure.id),,drop=FALSE]
  taxa<-sort(unique(as.vector(sets)))
  do.call(rbind,lapply(taxa,function(j) {
    incident<-ids[rowSums(sets==j)>0]
    members<-which(assignment %in% incident)
    data.frame(Vertex=fit$feature.labels[j],Degree=length(incident),
      n=length(unique(members)),Percent=100*length(unique(members))/length(assignment))
  }))
}
vertex.table<-taxon.stats(pair,g60$nodes$ID)
knitr::kable(vertex.table,digits=2,row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(vertex.table$n[vertex.table$Vertex=='A']==8L,
          vertex.table$Degree[vertex.table$Vertex=='A']==2L)
```

A has degree two and an incident-state union of eight observations. B has
five and C has three. A row can contribute to two endpoint vertices, so
**vertex percentages need not sum to 100%**. The denominator remains all
12 input observations. The table describes the selected graph as a whole;
clicking a vertex would not redefine these quantities.

For exclusive state assignments, incident-state counts can be summed without
double counting within one vertex. Explicit row unions also work when future
membership definitions overlap. Repeating the table with active absorbed
assignments answers a different question and must be labeled accordingly.

```{r toy-taxon-graph, echo=FALSE}
sets<-pair$feature.sets[match(g60$nodes$ID,pair$pure.id),,drop=FALSE]
taxa<-sort(unique(as.vector(sets))); a<-2*pi*seq_along(taxa)/length(taxa)
xy<-cbind(cos(a),sin(a),0)
edges<-matrix(match(sets,taxa),ncol=2)
ivue::plot3D.plain(xy,col='#C94845',point.type='sphere',sphere.radius=.065,
  axes=FALSE,xlab='',ylab='',zlab='',aspect='equal',height=410L,controls=FALSE,
  camera=ivue::camera.zup(elevation=70,turn=0,zoom=.85),
  layers=list(ivue::layer3D.edges(edges,col='#6C9AAF',width=2+4*g60$nodes$freq/max(g60$nodes$freq)),
    ivue::layer3D.labels(seq_along(taxa),colnames(X)[taxa],offset=c(0,.18,0))),
  description='Taxon graph at 60% requested coverage. Edges are A + B (5 observations) and A + C (3). Positions are schematic.')
```

## A pair-state graph needs different evidence

Now each vertex is a pair state. Two vertices such as A + B and A + C share
A; their unique common triple is A + B + C. Under `adjacency='observed_triple'`,
an edge is admitted only if **both** pair configurations occur among rows
whose pure top-3 set is that triple.

Write $I(P,T)$ for the number of rows with pure pair P and pure triple T.
With `min.support=1`, both $I(P,T)\geq1$ and $I(Q,T)\geq1$ are required.
Merely sharing a feature is the weaker alternative `adjacency='shared_feature'`.

```{r pair-graph}
g.all<-linf.udcst.graph(X,coverage=100)
candidate<-g.all$candidate.edges
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Pair A`=label.set(candidate$pair.a,pair),
  `Pair B`=label.set(candidate$pair.b,pair),Triple=label.set(candidate$triple,triple),
  `Support A`=candidate$i.a,`Support B`=candidate$i.b,
  Admitted=candidate$min.support>=1,check.names=FALSE),row.names=FALSE)
```

A + B and B + C share B, but the B + C observations have leading triple
B + C + D, not A + B + C. That edge therefore fails the observed-triple rule.
The full pair and triple frequencies remain the marginals even after graph
selection; selecting vertices does not renormalize them.

```{r pair-state-graph, echo=FALSE}
a<-2*pi*seq_len(nrow(g.all$nodes))/nrow(g.all$nodes)
xyz<-cbind(cos(a),sin(a),0)
ivue::plot3D.plain(xyz,col='#0072B2',point.type='sphere',sphere.radius=.065,
  axes=FALSE,xlab='',ylab='',zlab='',aspect='equal',height=430L,controls=FALSE,
  camera=ivue::camera.zup(elevation=70,turn=0,zoom=.95),
  layers=list(ivue::layer3D.edges(as.matrix(g.all$edges[,c('from','to')]),col='#6C9AAF',width=3),
    ivue::layer3D.labels(seq_len(nrow(xyz)),g.all$nodes$label,offset=c(0,.18,0))),
  description='Pair-state graph at 100% coverage with observed-triple support. Vertices are pair states, not taxa; isolates are retained.')
```

A witnessed triangular face requires all three pair configurations within
one common triple. A triangle assembled from different witnesses is not such
a face. This example has no witnessed faces. Edge `length` is one; support
and Jaccard columns are evidence attributes, not distances to pass unchanged
as path lengths. Neither graph proves a transition between communities.

## The same bookkeeping on valencia2k

We now use all 2,000 bundled observations and 178 taxon features. Each row
counts once; these are observation frequencies, not participant frequencies
or population prevalence. The data were stratified for teaching; see the
[dataset guide](https://pgajer.github.io/linf/articles/example-datasets.html).

```{r bundled}
data(valencia2k,package='linf')
P<-valencia2k$rel
p2<-linf.udcsts(P,2,1,'pure');p3<-linf.udcsts(P,3,1,'pure')
rows.with.zero.ranks<-sum(p3$positive.features<3)
tied.second<-sum(apply(P,1,function(x) {v<-sort(x,decreasing=TRUE);v[2]==v[3]}))
real.graphs<-lapply(c(60,80,90,100),function(q) linf.udcst.graph(pair.fit=p2,triple.fit=p3,coverage=q))
summary.table<-do.call(rbind,lapply(real.graphs,function(g) data.frame(
  Requested=g$metadata$requested.coverage,Achieved=g$metadata$coverage,
  Pair_states=nrow(g$nodes),Supported_edges=nrow(g$edges),
  Components=g$metadata$components,Isolates=g$metadata$isolates)))
knitr::kable(summary.table,digits=2,row.names=FALSE)
```

There are **`r rows.with.zero.ranks` rows with fewer than three positive taxa**
and **`r tied.second` ties across the second/third rank boundary**, including
zero ties. We retain the package's documented deterministic assignments and
report these counts rather than interpreting tie-broken ranks as certain.

```{r bundled-vertices}
g90<-real.graphs[[3]]
vertices90<-taxon.stats(p2,g90$nodes$ID)
vertices90<-vertices90[order(-vertices90$n,vertices90$Vertex),]
knitr::kable(head(vertices90,12),digits=2,row.names=FALSE)
stopifnot(sum(p2$frequency.table$freq)==nrow(P),sum(p3$frequency.table$freq)==nrow(P),
  all(vapply(real.graphs,function(g) g$metadata$reference.n==nrow(P),logical(1))),
  all(vertices90$n<=nrow(P)),nrow(g.all$faces)==0L)
```

This table describes **taxon vertices** in the selected pure pair-state
family at 90% requested coverage. The preceding table's `Pair_states` and
`Supported_edges` instead describe the pair-state graph. Using distinct
column names helps keep these representations separate.

## A practical reporting convention

Report the input population and counting unit, pure versus active assignment,
requested and achieved pure coverage, and which graph representation is shown.
Retain pure pair and triple IDs alongside any absorbed label. For vertex
unions, keep the denominator fixed and state whether assignments are pure or
absorbed. Describe the tie rule and retain the feature dictionary.

For VME datasets with reference-specific rank-3 or nearest-neighbor assignment
stages, the dataset's own construction record is authoritative. The generic
linf absorption example here must not be substituted silently for those rules.

This website article needs linf and ivue/rgl. Run `make state-graphs-vignette`
in the linf source checkout to render it and verify its counts. No private
VME dataset is needed, and no fitting, merging, or classifier is invoked
implicitly when the colors or drawing positions change.
